lesson.title: Squeeze and Push Back: Boyle's Law
lesson.summary: Boyle's law states that at constant temperature and amount of gas, pressure and volume are inversely related: as one goes up, the other goes down by the same factor.
lesson.body:
Boyle's law is what you get when you take the ideal gas law, PV = nRT, and hold both the temperature and the number of moles fixed. If n, R, and T are all constant, then nRT is just some constant number, which means PV must also equal that same constant number no matter how P and V individually change. This is usually written as P1V1 = P2V2, where the subscripts 1 and 2 refer to the gas before and after some change. The relationship this describes is an inverse one: squeeze a gas into a smaller volume and its pressure rises; let it expand into a larger volume and its pressure falls, always in a way that keeps the product PV constant.

The kinetic molecular picture explains why this has to be true. Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the container walls. If you shrink the container while keeping the temperature (and therefore the average particle speed) the same, the particles have less distance to travel between wall collisions, so they hit the walls more frequently. More collisions per second means more pressure. Nothing about the particles themselves changed, only how often they run into a wall, which is exactly what you would predict from gas pressure being a collision-frequency effect.

A worked example makes this concrete. Suppose a sample of gas occupies 5.00 L at a pressure of 1.20 atm, and you compress it at constant temperature until its volume is 2.00 L. What is the new pressure? Using P1V1 = P2V2: (1.20 atm)(5.00 L) = P2(2.00 L). The left side multiplies out to 6.00 L·atm. Solving for P2: P2 = 6.00 / 2.00 = 3.00 atm. The volume shrank to 2/5 of its original size, and the pressure correspondingly rose to 5/2 (or 2.5 times) its original value, confirming the inverse relationship: 1.20 atm times 2.5 is exactly 3.00 atm.

Boyle's law is a special case; it only applies when temperature and moles genuinely stay constant. If you compress a gas quickly, it often heats up as well, and that added temperature effect is layered on top of the pressure-volume relationship, requiring the full ideal gas law rather than the simplified P1V1 = P2V2 form. Recognizing when a problem describes a truly constant-temperature process is the key skill for knowing when Boyle's law applies cleanly.
